The verified buildings lining Boulevard Saint-Germain are six-storey Haussmann apartment blocks with uniform cream-coloured Lutetian limestone facades, regularly spaced tall windows, long running wrought-iron balconies on the noble floor and simpler balconies above [1]. Directly opposite stands the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, with the Café de Flore nearby at the corner of Boulevard Saint-Germain and Rue Saint-Benoît. The street is wide, paved with asphalt, marked lanes, sidewalks, plane trees, metro signs, street lamps and café awnings; writer Georges Perec recorded this same junction of Rue du Bac and Boulevard Saint-Germain on 15 May 1973 as a busy café-terrace observatory.

Ordinary daily life is café sitting, walking, shopping and commuting, with dense car traffic arriving in clumps after red lights. Period transport is almost entirely French: Renault, Citroën and Peugeot saloons, Citroën 2CVs and DS models, Renault city buses, bicycles and the metro; the final section of the Boulevard Périphérique ring road opened in 1973 after heavy use since 1967.
